chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
title: Jimmy Palao, sleeping Tinette, Keppard's prank and Willie Humphrey quitting
summary: At Harry Parker's, Palao's substitute Tinette fell asleep playing and Freddie Keppard greased his bow; Willie Humphrey Sr. quit after a row with a beer hustler and George Baquet replaced him.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: The musicians? And they didn't have no musicians. They didn't hang out? They didn't even bum in the barber shop? No. They bum around the 25-hour ballroom like that, you know. Not no barber shop, no. Well, what about Jimmy Palau? Now Jimmy Palau was a violin player. He was a good violin player. He played with me. Oh, yeah? Yeah, they played with me at Harry Park and Charlie Park. He played violin with me over there. They, uh, uh, they fired, uh, one time they, uh, they had gotten a humbug. He'd gotten a humbug with a woman around there in the place. Uh, Jim Palau laid off. I think he laid off from there one night. And he sent a tinette in his place. Uh-huh. Well, at that time, they had concessions. They had shops on the, on the, on the gutter side. Regular, little, regular little shop, where they make hamburgers. Like on the bank? No, right off, off, off, off the streets from the sidewalk. On the edge of the sidewalk. Right across the, to the edge. And you know, they made it this large enough for one woman to get in there, you know, fried pork chop and hamburgers. And they had a window. Like a markdown lady. Yeah, like a markdown. You could go to that window and get you a hamburger, a fried pork chop, sandwich, and all that. Well, they had plenty of demand for that. Well, T-Net, he, uh, he was a violin player. Uh, we opened up. And we start, first number, we start playing, he played alright. So the next number, when we got ready to play the next number, T-Net went, started going dodo. Start to sleeping. And, so, uh, Freddie Keppert, you know how, you know how, you see, there was, there was, he was a good kind, real, always after a whole lot of development, you know, all the time. So he went outside, they said, oh, again? So he had a way, he could play for all the good, but he'd sleep. He'd go to sleep right now. He didn't watch him. So, Freddie Keppert went over and got him a, a pork chop sandwich, you know, at the shop, and he took the fat, he took the fat off, he cut that little fat off the side of the pork chop and come on back in there. And he took, he took the violin bow, you know, and he breathed it with, and T-Net sitting up there sleeping, and we start the playing, you know. And after a while, T-Net jumped up and grabbed his bow, you know, and the bow was slipping over the violin, and he got his rosam out, and he started rosam, he put rosam all on his bow, and it was just slipping all the time. He said, it won't bite, it won't bite. So, so Parker the boss man come and stood up, you know, and see him. He was sawing on the violin, and he wasn't making no noise at all. He told me, he said, what's the last thing? I said, say he was sleeping, he said, pay him more. He was sleeping, go home and go to sleep. Now, the other fellow we had trouble with there. Freddie Keper was the one who did that. Yeah. Well, Freddie was full of demonstrate all the time, you know. He's just like a bad boy. Willie Umphrey, the old man, Willie Umphrey's daddy, good clarinet player. Willie had a humpback with a woman in there, in Parker's place one night, and she must have had something, she asked if he could play a drummer and he wouldn't play for her. She had some grudge against me. While we was playing in peace, you know, she had a chance to pick at Willie. She said something about his playing. Well, he was hot-headed. Old man Willie Umphrey was hot-headed. So, he said, I ain't gonna stand for this any longer. Boom! And I looked around, he done pulled his clarinet loose, you know, and packed it up. So, when he got through playing, I said, well, what's the matter, Willie? I quit. I said, oh, no, no, no. That man, they said, no, no. I don't want no trouble, I quit. So, I had to go and get his money behind the boy, and he quit. Willie Umphrey wasn't going two blocks, a half a block. Right cross was from there was 25's, borough at the corner. George Back A was in there. In fact, that was a plot. George Back A was in that borough with his clarinet. As soon as he saw Willie Umphrey going on the street, here he come. They put George Back A in his place. That's how come George Back A got. Playing farinet. And, uh, well, uh, must have been back here since then. That's been, yeah, that's been a long time. And he stayed there for after, he stayed with Willie Umphrey. But, well, I couldn't get Willie Umphrey. He was hot-headed. He said there wasn't nothing to do with him. But, she, she, she, she was the woman that he had a humbug with. She was one of the big stars in the place, you know, what you call a beer hustler. She was working for the place, you know. And you know how them beer hustlers is with the boss. They good, they fine looking and everything, you know. Anything they say, the boss, you know, she's got a skirt on. You know how it is. And so Willie just figured he, she had the best goal. And he said the best thing for him to do. And he was, always had a big pocket full of money. He always had a great big roll of money in his pocket. Who, Willie? Willie Umphrey. The old man. The old man had about four or five floats up in the, in the garden, up in the Irish Channel. That's where he come from. Cotton floats? Yeah, oh, them big old floats, which from, he used to haul stuff on the river. Yeah. Yeah, he, he used to run floats. Right. Yeah. That's Willie. He was great, huh? Yeah, well on. Had plenty of mules, plenty of hordes, mules and things, a big gang of floats and things. Always had a pocket full of money. Uh-huh. Well, he didn't have to play music then, huh? No, he didn't have to play. He just liked to play. This was good. He liked to play. Was he a playboy like? No, he had a family. He had a wife. Now Willie, Willie wasn't playing at that time. I don't believe Willie. The one that's playing trumpet now. He wasn't playing. He wasn't playing. One of them had a ballroom uptown there. I don't know whether it was Willie. Or one of them had a ballroom. I think it's Willie, though. Big Willie. We call it Big Willie. The clarinet player. Yeah, the one that's alive, no? Yeah, yeah. I think, I think he had the ballroom uptown. Long time ago. So now and then we'd run up there to his place.
